question: Why is systematic site rotation clinically necessary for patients receiving daily subcutaneous injections?

options.A: It maintains predictable drug absorption and prevents tissue damage
options.B: It completely eliminates the sensation of pain during insertion
options.C: It stops the immune system from developing systemic allergies
options.D: It prevents the needle from becoming dull during repeated use

explanation: Healthy, undamaged tissue ensures proper drug uptake, whereas scarred or fatty tissue alters pharmacokinetics. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T7#GNS125_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary skin layer targeted during an intradermal injection?

options.A: The dermis layer

question: Why is absorption significantly slower with intradermal injections?

options.A: Medications used are always oily suspensions
options.B: The needle depth blocks local circulation
options.C: The dermis has limited blood vessel supply
options.D: Skin cells in the dermis resist fluid

question: A Mantoux tuberculin skin test is administered via which route?

options.A: Intradermal route
options.B: Intravenous route
options.C: Subcutaneous route
options.D: Intramuscular route

question: A patient requires routine screening for tuberculosis exposure. Which action should the nurse take?

question: What is the maximum volume of medication typically given intradermally?

options.A: 0.5 mL
options.B: 1.0 mL

question: Which syringe type is standard for administering an intradermal injection?

question: What is the preferred anatomical site for a standard tuberculin skin test?

options.A: Lateral deltoid muscle region
options.B: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock

options.D: Anterior thigh muscle area

question: Why should a nurse avoid scarred skin areas when choosing an injection site?

options.A: Blood vessels in scars increase bleeding risk

options.C: Scar tissue alters absorption and obscures reactions

question: At what angle should the nurse insert the needle for an intradermal injection?

options.A: 60 to 75 degrees

question: Why is massaging the injection site discouraged after an intradermal injection?

question: What part of a tuberculin skin reaction is measured to determine a positive result?

question: A patient returns after 72 hours for a reading of their Mantoux test. What should the nurse assess?

question: What should the nurse do if no raised bleb appears during an intradermal injection?

question: Which complication is most associated with allergy skin testing?

question: What is the main benefit of giving medication directly into a joint space?

question: Why is keeping the area completely sterile so important during a joint injection?

options.A: Bacteria introduced into the joint space can cause septic arthritis

options.C: Joint cavities are prone to severe infections due to limited vascular supply
options.D: Unsterile technique immediately deactivates the administered steroid

question: Which type of drug is commonly injected into joints to bring down swelling and inflammation?

question: Viscosupplementation agents like hyaluronic acid are mostly used to manage which condition?

question: Which situation is a major reason NOT to perform a joint injection?

question: A patient scheduled for a knee joint injection takes warfarin. What should the nurse do first?

question: Which skin cleanser is most commonly used to prep the skin before a joint injection?

question: Why must skin antiseptic agents dry completely before the nurse inserts the needle?

options.C: To stop the patient from experiencing a burning sensation

question: What self-care advice is usually given to a patient right after a joint injection?

options.D: Massaging the injection site vigorously

question: What normal reaction can happen a few hours after a patient receives a joint steroid injection?

question: Which symptom helps a nurse tell the difference between a normal post-injection flare and septic arthritis?

question: A patient with diabetes notices high blood sugar readings at home after getting a joint steroid injection. What causes this?

options.B: Dietary indiscretion following the joint procedure
options.C: Inadequate skin preparation prior to the injection

question: What primary role does a nurse play in preventing drug errors?

question: System failures in medication safety usually involve which of the following?

options.D: Intentional harm caused by the medical staff

question: When should a nurse document that a medication was given?

question: Why must a nurse use two unique identifiers to check the right patient?

options.C: To check if the patient has health insurance

question: How should high-alert medications like narcotics be stored on the ward?

options.D: On top of the medication trolley in a basket

question: What is the main reason for using tall-man lettering on drug labels?

question: A patient is prescribed digoxin. What must the nurse check before giving this drug?

options.D: Respiratory rate

question: What is the primary purpose of checking patient allergies before drug administration?

options.C: To determine the patient's dietary food preferences
options.D: To calculate the correct financial bill for drugs

question: What practice must be avoided when preparing injectable medications?

question: Why is independent double-checking recommended for high-risk drug calculations?

question: Which type of tablet must never be crushed before administration?

question: Why must the nurse stay at the bedside until oral medications are swallowed?

question: What is the main purpose of post-administration monitoring?

question: How soon should a nurse monitor a patient after starting a new intravenous antibiotic?

question: What is the immediate priority when a medication error occurs?

options.B: Calling the pharmacy department to replace the drug

question: Why do hospitals use incident reports for medication mistakes?

question: What is the main purpose of enteric coating on certain oral medication tablets?

question: Which anatomical structure is the primary site for absorbing oral medications?

options.A: Small intestine
options.B: Large colon
options.C: Stomach lining
options.D: Esophagus

question: How does severe diarrhea typically affect the absorption of an oral prescription drug?

question: What is the biological term for the fraction of an administered drug that reaches systemic circulation unchanged?

question: Why does oral administration often result in lower drug concentration compared to intravenous administration?

question: A patient with a nasogastric tube needs an oral medication that is formulated as a sustained-release tablet. What is the appropriate nursing action?

question: Which nursing instruction is essential when administering an oral medication that binds to food in the stomach?

options.A: Mix the crushed tablet powder into dairy products to improve taste

options.C: Swallow the tablet immediately following a heavy, high-fat meal

explanation: Certain drugs interact with food components or require acid-free environments, making administration on an empty stomach necessary. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T1#GNS125_U5_T1_h7)

question: What four processes are included in the term drug disposition?

question: Why might a standard drug dose not work the same way for every patient?

question: Which kidney function consistently declines in older adults and affects how drugs leave the body?

options.A: Bladder detrusor tone

question: An increase in body fat in older adults changes how which type of drug is stored in the body?

options.A: Inorganic mineral salts
options.B: Protein-bound electrolytes
options.C: Lipid-soluble medications
options.D: Water-soluble medications

question: Grapefruit juice interacts with certain medications by blocking which specific enzyme in the gut?

question: Why does severe protein malnutrition increase the risk of drug toxicity for medications that bind to proteins in the blood?

options.A: It causes rapid renal elimination of the primary active metabolite

options.C: There are higher levels of free, unbound active drug floating in the bloodstream

explanation: Low albumin levels mean fewer binding sites exist, leaving a larger fraction of free drug active and available to cause toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h3)

question: Long-term exposure to industrial toxins in the workplace primarily alters how the body handles drugs by affecting which organ?

options.A: Liver
options.B: Pancreas
options.C: Spleen
options.D: Thyroid

explanation: The liver houses the primary metabolic enzymes responsible for processing xenobodies and toxins, making it the main organ affected by occupational exposures. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h4)

question: How does liver enzyme induction from industrial chemical exposure typically affect a patient's prescription drug needs?

options.A: Lower doses are required to prevent immediate kidney failure
options.B: Higher doses may be needed because the body clears the drug faster
options.C: Medications must be given exclusively through an IV line
options.D: Dosing remains unchanged because toxins do not affect pharmacokinetics

explanation: Upregulated liver enzymes break down medications more quickly, which can drop plasma levels below the therapeutic window. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h4)

question: What is the main effect of severe liver cirrhosis on how the body clears medications?

options.A: Immediate conversion of all drugs into inactive salts
options.B: Accelerated excretion through the biliary duct system
options.C: Decreased metabolism leading to drug buildup in the body
options.D: Complete elimination of first-pass gastrointestinal losses

explanation: Cirrhosis damages hepatic tissue and reduces enzyme production, which slows down metabolism and allows drugs to accumulate. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h5)

question: Why can a severe infection with high systemic inflammation change how a patient responds to medications?

options.A: Fever increases the rate of kidney filtration beyond normal limits
options.B: White blood cells actively bind to free drug molecules in the blood
options.C: Inflammatory signals slow down liver enzyme activity

question: Which lab values should a nurse check to assess a patient's ability to metabolize drugs?

options.A: Liver enzymes

question: A nurse reviews a new prescription for an elderly patient with kidney problems. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Administer the medication with a large glass of grapefruit juice

options.D: Instruct the patient to double the dose if symptoms do not improve

explanation: Elderly patients with kidney impairment often require adjusted doses to prevent drug accumulation and toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h6)

question: What is drug distribution defined as in pharmacokinetics?

options.A: The permanent breakdown of active drug molecules in the liver
options.B: The reversible transfer of a drug between body compartments
options.C: The complete elimination of waste products through the kidneys
options.D: The rate at which a tablet dissolves in the stomach

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs move quickly out of the bloodstream?

options.A: They repel water molecules in the body fluids

question: Which feature in standard blood vessels allows water-soluble drugs to leave the circulation?

options.A: Active energy pumps
options.B: Thick skin layers
options.C: Tiny pores between cells
options.D: Solid vessel walls

question: What makes it hard for a drug to cross strict barriers in the body?

options.A: Small size and high fat solubility
options.B: Large size and high water solubility
options.C: Strong attraction to red blood cells
options.D: Quick breakdown by blood enzymes

explanation: Large or water-soluble molecules cannot easily slip through tight cellular junctions without special transport. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which main blood protein is primarily responsible for binding acidic drugs?

options.A: Fibrinogen
options.B: Albumin
options.C: Hemoglobin

explanation: Albumin is the main circulating plasma protein that binds acidic and neutral drug molecules in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does a very high volume of distribution tell you about a drug?

options.A: It binds permanently to red blood cells
options.B: It spreads heavily into body tissues
options.C: It leaves the body immediately through urine
options.D: It stays strictly inside the blood plasma

question: Why might a doctor order a larger starting dose for a drug that spreads heavily into body tissues?

options.A: Most of the drug leaves the blood and goes into storage sites

options.C: The kidneys remove the entire dose too fast
options.D: The drug turns into crystals inside blood vessels

explanation: When a drug hides in tissues, a larger initial dose is needed to achieve effective therapeutic levels in the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which group of organs receives a drug the fastest right after it enters the bloodstream?

options.A: Skin, bones, and tendons
options.B: Fat tissue and resting skeletal muscle
options.C: Cartilage and joints
options.D: Brain, heart, liver, and kidneys

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs tend to build up in body fat over time?

options.A: Fat tissue has low blood flow and stores fat-loving compounds well
options.B: Blood flow to fat is higher than to the brain
options.C: Fat cells pull drugs inward using active pumps
options.D: Fat tissue turns the drug into solid crystals

question: What feature of the blood-brain barrier stops water-soluble drugs from entering the brain?

question: What is the main concern when a pregnant woman takes medications that cross the placenta?

question: How does severe malnutrition affect how drugs behave in the body?

options.A: Dehydration greatly expands total body fluid volume

question: A dehydrated child with severe diarrhea gets a standard dose of a water-soluble antibiotic. What is the likely result of having less fluid in the body?

question: Why might a fat-soluble drug that spreads widely through the body stay active for a long time?

question: An older adult with changes in body fat is given a fat-soluble sedative. What should the nurse watch out for?

question: What is the main goal of drug metabolism in the body?

question: How does a prodrug differ from a standard active drug?

question: Which organ is the main site for drug metabolism?

question: Besides the liver, which other part of the body plays a big role in breaking down drugs before they enter general circulation?

question: What is the main chemical result of a Phase I metabolic reaction?

question: Where are Cytochrome P450 enzymes mostly found inside liver cells?

question: Why do genetic differences in CYP450 enzymes matter for patient care?

question: What happens when a patient takes an enzyme-inducing drug along with a regular medication?

question: What is it called when one drug blocks the metabolic enzyme activity of another drug?

question: What term describes the amount of an unchanged drug that actually reaches the general bloodstream?

question: Why do oral medications often need a higher dose than drugs given through a vein?

question: Which of these is NOT a reason why drug processing varies among different populations?

question: Why must nurses ask patients if they are taking traditional herbal remedies?

question: What is the primary organ responsible for eliminating water-soluble drugs from the body?

question: Why are gases like inhaled anesthetics mainly breathed out through the lungs?

question: Which type of drug molecules can pass through the kidney's tiny filtering units?

question: For a drug to stay trapped in the kidney tubes and be passed out in urine, what property must it have?

question: How does making a patient's urine more alkaline affect weak acid medications?

question: Why do older adults often need lower doses of drugs that are cleared by the kidneys?

options.C: Their active kidney secretion works much faster

question: Where do drugs that are excreted through the biliary system eventually end up?

question: What happens when a drug goes through enterohepatic recirculation in the body?

question: Which way of eliminating drugs from the body can pose a direct risk to a nursing infant?

question: Why does the alcohol in a person's breath match the level of alcohol in their blood?

question: What does a drug's half-life mean in clinical practice?

question: How does severe kidney failure affect a drug's elimination half-life?

options.C: It stops drug breakdown in the stomach entirely
options.D: It makes the half-life longer because the drug leaves the body slower

question: Which lab test do nurses usually check to see how well a patient's kidneys are clearing drugs?

question: Why do nurses closely monitor patients with kidney problems who are taking drugs cleared by the kidneys?

question: What is the primary focus of pharmacodynamics?

question: Which agency in Nigeria is primarily responsible for receiving reports on adverse drug reactions?

options.A: FMOH
options.B: NAFDAC

options.D: NCDC

explanation: NAFDAC handles pharmacovigilance and tracks adverse drug reactions nationwide in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T9#GNS125_U5_T9_h7)

question: Why is detailed charting of an unusual drug reaction in a patient's record so vital?

options.A: It guarantees the patient will never need any medication again
options.B: It prevents future healthcare providers from giving the dangerous drug again
options.C: It allows the hospital to bill the pharmaceutical company for damages
options.D: It proves the nurse followed every hospital protocol correctly

explanation: Clear charting ensures that everyone on the healthcare team knows the patient is dangerously sensitive to that specific drug. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T9#GNS125_U5_T9_h7)

question: What is the main goal of a National Health Policy?

options.A: To exclusively control pharmaceutical manufacturing prices
options.B: To outline healthcare priorities and resource allocation strategies
options.C: To license private medical practitioners across the country
options.D: To manage hospital infrastructure funding in rural areas

explanation: A National Health Policy sets the main framework for national healthcare needs, guiding how resources and services are distributed to improve public health. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must the National Drug Policy match closely with the National Health Policy?

options.A: Medications are essential tools needed to achieve broader health goals
options.B: Drug policies operate independently from clinical health interventions
options.C: Hospitals cannot purchase equipment without prior drug policy clearance
options.D: Pharmaceutical companies fund the implementation of national health budgets

explanation: Good healthcare needs medicines, so drug policies must line up with overall health goals to successfully treat illnesses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: When was Nigeria's very first National Drug Policy launched?
explanation: Nigeria introduced its first official National Drug Policy in 1990 to fight fake drugs and chaotic drug importation. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: What major problem led to the creation of early drug policies in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive government funding for international drug importation
options.B: A complete lack of qualified doctors in urban teaching hospitals
options.C: Rampant fake products and an unregulated open drug market
options.D: An absolute surplus of locally manufactured pharmaceutical products

explanation: Unregulated open drug markets and fake medications caused serious health crises, prompting the government to create official drug policies. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a main goal of the National Drug Policy?

options.A: Eliminating all private pharmacies from urban areas
options.B: Promoting the rational use of essential medicines
options.C: Mandating free herbal remedies in tertiary hospitals
options.D: Increasing international importation of luxury cosmetics

explanation: Rational drug use ensures patients get the right medicines for their clinical needs at the correct doses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why is boosting local drug manufacturing a key goal in Nigeria's drug policy?

options.A: To ensure that nurses can manufacture intravenous fluids in wards
options.B: To reduce heavy reliance on foreign drug importation and stabilize supply
options.C: To completely ban foreign pharmaceutical companies from operating locally
options.D: To eliminate the need for quality control regulatory agencies

explanation: Making drugs locally protects the country from global supply shortages and foreign exchange price changes. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which agency handles drug manufacturing and importation rules in Nigeria?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: PHCC
options.C: NMNC
options.D: FMOH

explanation: NAFDAC stands for the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, which monitors drug safety and manufacturing standards. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the specific role of the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria?

options.A: Manufacturing essential vaccines for rural primary healthcare centers
options.B: Regulating the training and professional practice of pharmacists
options.C: Conducting clinical trials on new surgical techniques in teaching hospitals
options.D: Setting international pricing standards for imported medical equipment

explanation: The Pharmacists Council of Nigeria handles professional standards, licensing, and training for pharmacy staff rather than checking manufactured products. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: How are essential medicines defined in national health and drug policies?

options.A: Medicines that satisfy the priority healthcare needs of the population
options.B: Traditional herbal extracts prepared by local community healers
options.C: Experimental medications tested only in tertiary research institutions
options.D: Expensive brand-name drugs imported exclusively from Western countries

explanation: Essential medicines are chosen based on common illnesses, safety, how well they work, and affordability. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: A patient cannot afford prescribed antibiotics out of pocket. Which policy helps fix this issue?

options.A: Direct referral to private international pharmaceutical consultants
options.B: Increasing import tariffs on raw pharmaceutical ingredients
options.C: National Health Insurance Authority coverage schemes
options.D: Immediate suspension of local generic drug manufacturing plants

explanation: Health insurance helps protect patients from heavy out-of-pocket costs by covering or subsidizing essential medicines. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: What technology helps patients check if their drugs are real in Nigeria?

options.A: Microscopic chemical analysis at patient bedsides
options.B: Mandatory DNA sequencing at local retail pharmacies
options.C: Biometric fingerprint scanning for medication purchase
options.D: Mobile SMS scratch-card verification systems

question: Why are fake or substandard drugs very dangerous for treating infections?

options.A: They foster antimicrobial resistance and cause treatment failure
options.B: They immediately cure infections without requiring medical supervision
options.C: They eliminate the need for diagnostic laboratory testing in clinics
options.D: They reduce the cost of healthcare services for impoverished patients

explanation: Substandard drugs have weak active ingredients, which fail to kill germs and instead help germs build resistance to future treatments. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do nurses help with national pharmacovigilance?

options.A: By manufacturing intravenous replacement fluids in hospital wards
options.B: By setting the retail prices for generic drugs in community pharmacies
options.C: By reporting adverse drug reactions to regulatory authorities
options.D: By importing essential medications directly from foreign manufacturers

explanation: Pharmacovigilance is about tracking and reporting bad drug reactions, and frontline nurses play a big role in spotting and reporting them. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h7)

question: A nurse sees that new oxytocin vials do not have NAFDAC registration numbers. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Administer the medication quickly before supervisors notice the anomaly
options.B: Sell the unregistered vials to patients at a discounted hospital price
options.C: Store the medication in the ward refrigerator for emergency use only
options.D: Quarantine the batch and report it through institutional channels

question: What primary factor guides the selection of essential drugs for a population?

options.A: Global marketing popularity
options.B: Advanced chemical complexity
options.C: Manufacturer profit margins
options.D: Priority health care needs

explanation: Essential drugs focus specifically on addressing the most common and critical health problems faced by the majority of the population. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why must essential medicines remain affordable within a community?

options.A: To increase the import taxes on foreign companies
options.B: To guarantee high profits for local pharmacies
options.C: To discourage patients from visiting traditional healers
options.D: To prevent out-of-pocket financial ruin for patients

question: In what year did the World Health Organization publish the first essential drug list?
explanation: The landmark WHO Expert Committee meeting in 1977 established the very first model list containing around 200 active substances. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h2)

question: What main problem led to the creation of the essential drugs concept?

options.A: An excessive drop in pharmaceutical manufacturing companies
options.B: A sudden global shortage of basic chemical raw materials
options.C: Markets flooded with redundant and unproven brand-name drugs
options.D: The total collapse of international shipping lanes

explanation: Developing nations were wasting scarce resources on thousands of unnecessary and expensive brand-name medications before standardisation. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h2)

question: How often does the WHO typically review and update its Model List of Essential Medicines?

options.A: Every six months
options.B: Every decade
options.C: Every two years
options.D: Every five years

explanation: Regular biennial reviews allow the WHO to incorporate new scientific breakthroughs and drop obsolete pharmaceutical agents. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which factor is NOT evaluated when deciding to add a drug to the essential list?

options.A: The public health relevance of the targeted disease
options.B: The scientific evidence supporting safety and efficacy
options.C: The overall cost-effectiveness of the treatment
options.D: The marketing budget of the manufacturing company

explanation: Selection committees rely strictly on clinical evidence, public health needs, and cost-effectiveness rather than commercial marketing budgets. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h3)

question: How does an essential drug list improve safety for clinical staff?

options.A: By replacing traditional nursing documentation with automated software

options.C: By completely eliminating the need for nurses to administer injections
options.D: By shifting all diagnostic responsibilities away from primary care clinics

question: What financial benefit does bulk-purchasing a limited set of medicines provide to health systems?

question: Why might a rigid essential drug list fail to meet all community needs during a health transition?

options.C: It forces manufacturing companies to shut down local factories
options.D: It prevents nurses from administering basic first aid

question: What common supply chain issue compromises heat-sensitive medicines in resource-limited settings?

question: What is the primary document derived from the National Drug Policy for public health facilities in Nigeria?

question: How does local pharmaceutical manufacturing support the goals of Nigeria's National Drug Policy?

question: What is the primary goal of the Essential Drug Programme?

options.D: Maximizing profits for private pharmaceutical importers

question: Why does the health system restrict the number of pharmaceutical variants stocked?

question: When did the World Health Organization publish the first model list of essential medicines?

question: How often does the WHO update its model list of essential medicines?

question: Which factor is NOT one of the core pillars of the essential drugs concept?

question: Who conducts the evaluation and selection of medicines for national formularies?

question: What is a common consequence of poor cold-chain storage in public health supply chains?

question: Which Nigerian agency conducts post-market surveillance to combat falsified medications?

question: What is a direct consequence of the widespread irrational use of broad-spectrum antibiotics?

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility related to hospital ward medications?

question: How do bedside nurses contribute directly to national pharmacovigilance?

question: What does a single unit package in a unit dose system contain?

question: A patient refuses to take a scheduled oral medication during the ward round. What should the nurse do with the unadministered unit dose?

question: Which factor contributes most to reduced drug wastage in a unit dose system?

question: Why does a unit dose system help decrease medication administration errors by nurses?

question: What is the primary purpose of the Nigerian National Formulary?

question: Why does the formulary emphasize International Non-proprietary Names?

question: What is the legal consequence of using medications outside formulary guidelines in public institutions?

question: A key factor for including a drug in the formulary is its relevance to what?

question: Why are expensive drugs with low comparative advantage often excluded from the formulary?

question: What practice involves giving patients more medications than are clinically necessary?

question: How does the formulary help combat antimicrobial resistance in Nigerian hospitals?

question: A nurse receives an unfamiliar drug order for a pediatric patient. What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.C: Ask another patient in the ward if they know the drug

question: What is the main goal of the Essential Drug Programme in Nigeria?

question: Why does the healthcare system focus on a specific list of essential medicines?

options.A: To make drug manufacturing easier for local herbalists

options.C: To maximize scarce financial resources for priority health needs
options.D: To completely stop the importation of foreign medical goods

question: What data helps nurses and pharmacists calculate accurate drug quantification needs?

question: A ward nurse notices a sudden spike in malaria cases during the rainy season. What action supports proper quantification?

question: What does the FEFO inventory principle stand for in pharmacy supply management?

options.A: Fast-Evaluation, Fast-Ordering

options.C: Foreign-Equipment, Facility-Operation
options.D: First-Expired, First-Out

question: Why must ward nurses regularly check and record storage temperatures for vaccines and insulins?

options.C: To make the pharmacy store room look neat and organized

question: What is a major consequence of the irrational use and overprescription of antibiotics?

options.A: Lower financial costs for the patient family

question: A nurse is about to give a medication prescribed by the doctor. Which check is essential to promote rational and safe drug use?

options.C: Ignoring hospital treatment guidelines to save time

question: Why do patients frequently stop taking their prescribed medications prematurely?

question: How can a nurse best support a patient who is confused about taking multiple daily medications?

options.A: Hiding the pill bottles to reduce the patient anxiety

question: What is the primary purpose of pharmacovigilance in healthcare?

question: A patient develops a severe skin rash shortly after receiving a newly introduced antibiotic. What is the immediate nursing duty?

question: What is the main goal of the National Drug Policy regarding how medicines are used?

question: A patient receives three different antibiotics for a simple cold caused by a virus. What do we call this practice?

options.D: Prophylactic therapy

question: Giving a patient two different drugs that belong to the exact same pharmacological class at the same time is known as:

question: A patient takes ibuprofen and indomethacin at the same time for joint pain. Both are pain relievers from the same drug family. What issue does this prescription show?

question: What is a common reason why clinicians sometimes feel pressured to prescribe medicines that a patient does not actually need?

question: Why does not knowing the exact cause of an illness often lead to unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions?

question: What major public health problem is directly made worse by the excessive use of antibiotics?

question: An elderly patient who is taking many unnecessary medications is at the highest risk for which of these problems?

question: What is the main purpose of nursing medication reconciliation?

question: A nurse notices a patient has been taking a sleeping pill every night for two years without a check-up. What is the best action to take?

question: Which Nigerian agency is mainly responsible for regulating drug safety and distribution?

question: Why do hospitals set up antimicrobial stewardship programs?

question: What defines drug under-prescription in clinical practice?

question: Which group of patients is most often affected by under-prescription?

question: What is a core requirement of rational prescribing?

question: What is the main goal of pharmacovigilance?

question: What is the most common problem facing drug safety systems around the world?

options.C: By guaranteeing that adverse drug reactions never happen again

explanation: Electronic tools and algorithms can process large volumes of patient data rapidly to detect unexpected drug signals early. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T1#GNS215_U2_T1_h7)

question: What does a patient drug history primarily record?

options.A: All current and recent substances taken
options.B: Family history of chronic illnesses
options.C: Only medications prescribed by a doctor
options.D: Surgical procedures from past admissions

explanation: A complete drug history captures every substance the patient ingests, including prescriptions and self-care remedies. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is gathering a drug history vital upon hospital admission?

options.A: It prevents potential drug interactions and adverse events
options.B: It replaces the need for a physical examination
options.C: It determines the final medical diagnosis
options.D: It reduces the length of hospital stay

explanation: Knowing current drug use helps clinicians avoid dangerous drug conflicts and unrecognized toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which detail is essential when recording a patient's medication dose?

options.A: Exact strength and frequency
options.B: Name of the manufacturing company
options.C: Cost of the prescription
options.D: Pharmacy location of purchase

explanation: Dosage and frequency define how much active substance enters the body and how often, which is critical for safe dosing. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient reports taking a drug for malaria prevention. What component of the drug history does this represent?

options.A: Allergy
options.B: Duration
options.C: Route
options.D: Indication

explanation: The reason why a drug is taken, such as preventing malaria, is classified as its indication. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the main benefit of using open-ended questions during medication interviews?

options.A: It prevents patients from asking questions
options.B: It shortens the time needed for the interview
options.C: It encourages patients to share accurate details freely
options.D: It eliminates the need for physical pill inspection

explanation: Open-ended questions stop patients from simply saying yes and prompt them to explain their actual habits. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the brown bag method in nursing assessment?

options.A: Storing waste medical supplies in paper bags
options.B: Having patients bring all their physical medicine containers
options.C: Disposing of expired tablets safely
options.D: Carrying hospital equipment in a brown sack

explanation: The brown bag method involves patients bringing their actual medication packs to the clinic for verification. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why do patients frequently omit herbal remedies from their drug history?

options.A: They do not view them as real medicine
options.B: Traditional mixtures lack active chemicals
options.C: Doctors explicitly forbid talking about herbs
options.D: Herbal products never cause side effects

explanation: Patients often separate orthodox drugs from herbs and supplements in their minds, forgetting to mention them unless probed. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is a major clinical risk of undocumented herbal medicine use?

options.A: Elimination of all nutritional deficiencies
options.B: Unexpected interactions with prescribed orthodox drugs
options.C: Automatic reduction in hospital bed costs
options.D: Guaranteed immediate cure of chronic diseases

explanation: Herbs contain active chemical compounds that can clash with prescription drugs and alter therapeutic outcomes. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: A patient admits to skipping doses of expensive hypertension medication to make it last longer. What primary barrier is present?

options.A: Financial constraint
options.B: Poor eyesight
options.C: Complex schedule
options.D: Cultural belief

explanation: Inability to afford drugs forces patients to ration their supplies, which is a financial barrier to adherence. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which approach helps a patient feel safe admitting poor medication adherence?

options.A: Assuming they follow all instructions perfectly
options.B: Using non-judgmental and open communication
options.C: Scolding them for missing past doses
options.D: Threatening to discharge them from the clinic

explanation: Patients hide non-adherence when nurses judge or scold them, so an open approach is essential. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: Where should the verified medication history be recorded for the healthcare team?

options.A: A private diary belonging to the patient
options.B: Scraps of paper discarded after the shift
options.C: A personal notebook kept in the nurse's pocket
options.D: The patient's official medical record and care plan

explanation: Official medical records ensure all multidisciplinary team members access safe, verified medication data. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h6)

question: What action should a nurse take upon discovering a drug discrepancy during reconciliation?

options.A: Ignore it if the patient seems stable enough
options.B: Report it immediately to the prescriber or pharmacist
options.C: Wait until the patient is discharged to mention it
options.D: Change the prescription independently without authority

explanation: Discrepancies require prompt interprofessional communication to correct errors before harm occurs. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of drug information in clinical practice?

options.A: Speeding up patient discharge times
options.B: Reducing hospital pharmacy expenses
options.C: Replacing the role of clinical pharmacists
options.D: Ensuring safe and effective medication use

explanation: Drug information focuses on providing accurate data to promote safe, effective medication administration and prevent errors. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why must nurses rely on current scientific evidence rather than memory alone?

options.A: Memory is completely unreliable after night shifts
options.B: Hospital management mandates reading journals daily
options.C: Pharmacological guidelines and safety profiles update frequently
options.D: Physicians expect nurses to memorize pharmacology textbooks

explanation: New clinical trials and safety warnings continuously emerge, making ongoing reference to updated drug information vital for patient safety. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which resource is classified as a tertiary source of drug information?

options.A: A standard pharmacology textbook
options.B: An unpublished hospital case report
options.C: An individual randomized controlled trial
options.D: A PubMed database search engine

explanation: Textbooks and formularies summarize established medical knowledge, placing them in the tertiary information tier. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h2)

question: A nurse needs a quick, summarized overview of a drug's standard dosage. Which source tier is best to check first?

options.A: Tertiary source
options.B: Secondary source
options.C: Unpublished source
options.D: Primary source

question: What is the first step when responding to a specific drug information query?

options.A: Consulting the senior hospital pharmacist
options.B: Searching online primary clinical trials
options.C: Writing the final patient education leaflet
options.D: Securing demographic and background details

explanation: Knowing the patient's specific clinical context is essential before evaluating any medication literature. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why should a nurse search tertiary sources before primary trials for a basic query?

options.A: Tertiary books are always written by local physicians
options.B: Primary journals are banned in most Nigerian teaching hospitals
options.C: Primary trials never contain relevant dosage information
options.D: Tertiary sources provide summarized, easily accessible consensus data

explanation: Starting with summarized sources saves time and usually answers standard clinical questions without sorting through raw trial data. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does critical appraisal of a clinical study primarily involve?

options.A: Examining methodology, statistics, and potential biases
options.B: Checking the publication fee paid by authors
options.C: Counting the number of pages in the journal
options.D: Verifying the academic title of the lead researcher

explanation: Critical appraisal requires evaluating how a study was conducted and analyzed to judge its scientific validity. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why must nurses consider local patient demographics when reading international clinical trials?

options.A: Treatment efficacy and safety can vary across different populations
options.B: Local hospital policy forbids foreign drug protocols
options.C: International trials never include adult patients
options.D: Foreign journals use different metric units for weight

explanation: Genetic, environmental, and healthcare infrastructure differences mean study results may not apply directly to every local patient. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h4)

question: How do nurses function within the medication safety network?

options.A: As the final safety barrier before drug administration
options.B: As the primary authors of clinical research trials
options.C: As the sole manufacturers of intravenous fluids
options.D: As the legal regulators of pharmaceutical imports

explanation: Nurses perform final checks and monitor patient responses right before and after medication administration. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h5)

question: A nurse notices an unusual skin rash after administering a newly prescribed antibiotic. What action reflects the nurse's drug information role?

options.A: Waiting until the end of the month to mention it
options.B: Administering the next scheduled dose immediately
options.C: Ignoring the rash if the patient feels slightly better
options.D: Reporting the adverse reaction and checking reference guidelines

question: What is the teach-back method in patient education?

options.A: Reviewing textbook chapters with student nurses
options.B: Reading the hospital drug formulary aloud to the patient
options.C: Asking patients to repeat medication instructions in their own words
options.D: Having the doctor test the nurse on drug dosages

explanation: The teach-back method checks patient comprehension by having them explain instructions back to the nurse. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why is assessing a patient's health literacy important before giving drug information?

options.A: It determines how much hospital bill the patient can pay
options.B: It helps tailor explanations to the patient's level of understanding
options.C: It proves whether the patient completed secondary school
options.D: It dictates which pharmaceutical company manufactured the drug

explanation: Matching the communication style to the patient's literacy level ensures safe and accurate medication use at home. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h6)

question: What legal consequence can arise from providing unverified medication advice that harms a patient?

options.A: Immediate hospital budget increase
options.B: Mandatory promotion to supervisor
options.C: Automatic research grant awards
options.D: Professional negligence claims

explanation: Nurses are legally liable for the accuracy of guidance provided, and sharing negligent advice can result in legal action. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is patient confidentiality critical when discussing medication histories?

options.A: It stops doctors from reviewing patient charts
options.B: It respects patient autonomy and builds clinical trust
options.C: It prevents pharmacy staff from ordering stock
options.D: It removes the need for proper documentation

explanation: Protecting patient privacy is a fundamental ethical duty that fosters trust between patients and healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T3#GNS215_U2_T3_h7)

question: What defines a drug interaction in clinical nursing practice?

options.A: The physical mixing of two medications in the same syringe
options.B: The standard therapeutic outcome of a single medication
options.C: An alteration in drug effect due to another substance
options.D: An allergic reaction triggered by the first dose of a drug

explanation: A drug interaction happens when a substance changes how a medication works in the body. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is identifying potential drug interactions crucial for ward nurses?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing medications
options.B: To speed up the routine morning medication round
options.C: To prevent treatment failures and unexpected drug toxicity
options.D: To eliminate the need for physician medication orders

explanation: Recognizing interactions early stops patients from suffering harmful side effects or failing to respond to therapy. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which ADME process is primarily affected by liver enzyme induction?

options.A: Metabolism
options.B: Absorption
options.C: Distribution
options.D: Excretion

question: What happens when a highly protein-bound drug is displaced from albumin?

options.A: Hepatic metabolism slows down to protect the kidney tissues
options.B: The total drug concentration in the body immediately drops to zero
options.C: Free active drug concentration in the bloodstream temporarily rises
options.D: Renal excretion stops completely due to molecular blockage

explanation: Displacement leaves more unbound drug free to exert pharmacological effects, raising toxicity risks. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h2)

question: What occurs during a pharmacodynamic drug antagonism?

options.A: Two drugs combine to create a much stronger therapeutic response
options.B: Both medications bind identical plasma proteins simultaneously
options.C: One drug prolongs the elimination half-life of another agent
options.D: One drug blocks or reduces the effect of another drug

explanation: Antagonistic agents work against each other at receptor sites to cancel or reduce effects. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h3)

question: How does synergism differ from simple drug addition?

options.A: Only one medication reaches the target receptor site in the tissue
options.B: It consistently decreases the risk of adverse drug reactions
options.C: The interaction occurs exclusively within the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: The combined effect is greater than the sum of individual effects

explanation: Synergistic combinations multiply therapeutic outcomes beyond standard additive expectations. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h3)

question: Grapefruit juice interacts with certain medications primarily by affecting which process?

options.A: Pulmonary gas exchange
options.B: Plasma protein binding
options.C: Intestinal drug metabolism
options.D: Renal tubular reabsorption

explanation: Grapefruit juice inhibits gut wall enzymes, increasing the amount of drug that enters the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why must patients on warfarin regulate their intake of green leafy vegetables?

options.A: Vegetables speed up the renal clearance of oral anticoagulant drugs
options.B: Dietary fiber stops the liver from metabolizing blood thinners
options.C: Green vegetables bind directly to warfarin molecules in the stomach
options.D: Vitamin K in greens can counteract the anticoagulant effect of the drug

explanation: Vitamin K promotes blood clotting, which directly opposes the action of vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h4)

question: What term describes the concurrent use of multiple medications by a single patient?

options.A: Pharmacovigilance
options.B: Bioavailability
options.C: Tachyphylaxis
options.D: Polypharmacy

explanation: Polypharmacy refers to taking multiple drugs, which sharply increases the chance of adverse interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why are elderly patients particularly susceptible to adverse drug interactions?

options.A: Their liver enzyme systems are permanently hyperactive
options.B: They lack plasma albumin proteins entirely throughout old age
options.C: Their gastrointestinal tracts absorb all medications much faster than adults
options.D: They frequently experience reduced hepatic blood flow and renal clearance

explanation: Decreased organ function slows down drug processing, causing drugs and metabolites to accumulate. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a medication reconciliation upon patient admission?

options.A: To create a complete and accurate list of all current medications
options.B: To calculate the total financial cost of hospital treatment
options.C: To test the patient's memory regarding past surgical procedures
options.D: To replace all traditional herbal remedies with prescription drugs

explanation: Reconciliation compares what the patient was taking at home with new orders to prevent omission or duplication errors. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h6)

question: A patient taking digoxin and a potassium-wasting diuretic is at risk for toxicity. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?

options.A: Serum potassium
options.B: Serum calcium
options.C: Blood glucose
options.D: Hemoglobin count

explanation: Low potassium levels heighten myocardial sensitivity to digoxin, leading to severe digitalis toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is a key nursing action to prevent absorption-based drug interactions?

options.A: Crushing all enteric-coated tablets together in liquid suspension
options.B: Administering every scheduled medication on an empty stomach
options.C: Staggering the administration times of interacting oral medications
options.D: Mixing multiple intravenous infusions into a single primary line

explanation: Separating administration times prevents drugs from binding to each other within the gastrointestinal tract. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h7)

question: How do hospital pharmacovigilance activities contribute to community safety?

options.A: By tracking and reporting adverse drug reactions to regulatory agencies
options.B: By conducting clinical trials on healthy volunteers before drug approval
options.C: By enforcing strict financial penalties for medication administration errors
options.D: By manufacturing safer generic alternatives to expensive imported drugs

explanation: Pharmacovigilance monitors safety data post-market to catch rare or unexpected adverse reactions early. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T4#GNS215_U2_T4_h7)

question: What defines an adverse drug reaction compared to a normal drug action?

options.A: It disappears without altering the dose.
options.B: It only happens when a patient overdoses.
options.C: It is harmful and occurs at normal doses.
options.D: It is a planned therapeutic outcome.

explanation: Adverse drug reactions are harmful and unexpected responses that happen even when the drug is taken correctly at standard doses. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why must a nurse separate a routine side effect from an adverse drug reaction?

options.A: Adverse reactions often demand a change in therapy.
options.B: Routine side effects are always fatal to patients.
options.C: Adverse reactions only occur in pediatric wards.
options.D: Side effects never require nursing documentation.

explanation: Unlike mild side effects that patients tolerate, true adverse reactions usually force the clinician to stop or switch the medication. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: What characterizes a Type A adverse drug reaction?

options.A: It is caused by sudden immune allergies.
options.B: It never occurs with standard drug doses.
options.C: It is completely unrelated to pharmacology.
options.D: It is dose-dependent and predictable.

explanation: Type A reactions stem from the primary pharmacological effect of the medication and happen more often when doses are high. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: An unexpected allergic rash develops after a standard dose of an antibiotic. What reaction type is this?

options.A: Expected therapeutic response
options.B: Primary pharmacological toxicity
options.C: Type A augmented reaction
options.D: Type B bizarre reaction

explanation: Allergic reactions do not depend on the drug dose and happen unpredictably in susceptible individuals, fitting the Type B category. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which patient group is most vulnerable to drug accumulation and adverse reactions?

options.A: Athletes with high muscle mass ratios
options.B: Healthy young adults with fast metabolism
options.C: Teenagers taking short-term antibiotics
options.D: Older adults with decreased renal clearance

explanation: Declining kidney and liver function in older adults slows down drug elimination, making them prone to toxic build-up. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient with severe liver cirrhosis is prescribed a drug cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism. What is the main risk?

options.A: The drug will immediately cure the liver disease.
options.B: The drug will accumulate and cause toxicity.
options.C: The drug will pass through without any effect.
options.D: The patient will develop an instant antibiotic allergy.

explanation: Liver damage stops proper drug breakdown, causing high blood levels of the medication and severe adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why must nurses ask about herbal remedies when assessing for adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Patients usually take herbs instead of modern medicines.
options.B: Herbs can interact with prescription drugs to cause toxicity.
options.C: Herbal products replace the need for hospital laboratory tests.
options.D: Traditional herbs never cause any adverse side effects.

explanation: Many patients combine orthodox drugs with local herbs, which can alter drug metabolism and trigger unexpected adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: A patient develops a sudden skin rash two hours after receiving a new intravenous antibiotic. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Stop the infusion and notify the prescriber.
options.B: Document the rash and wait for the next shift.
options.C: Give a standard dose of oral paracetamol.
options.D: Increase the fluid flow rate to dilute the drug.

explanation: Stopping the suspected drug immediately prevents further exposure and reduces the severity of an adverse reaction. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary management step when a severe adverse drug reaction occurs?

options.A: Double the dose to build patient immunity.
options.B: Switch the patient to a traditional herbal remedy.
options.C: Discontinue the suspected medication immediately.
options.D: Wait for laboratory confirmation before acting.

explanation: Removing the source of the reaction stops further harm and allows stabilization to begin. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: How does medication reconciliation at hospital admission prevent adverse drug reactions?

options.A: It eliminates the need for daily vital sign checks.
options.B: It guarantees the patient will take drugs on time.
options.C: It catches duplicate therapies and potential drug clashes.
options.D: It lowers the financial cost of purchasing drugs.

explanation: Comparing a patient's home medications with new hospital orders prevents dangerous interactions and accidental overdoses. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which Nigerian agency is responsible for regulating drugs and monitoring adverse reactions?

options.A: FMOH
options.B: NMA
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: NMCN

explanation: The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control handles drug safety surveillance and pharmacovigilance in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of submitting a yellow form to the national pharmacovigilance center?

options.A: To apply for nursing license renewal
options.B: To report suspected adverse drug reactions
options.C: To request free drug supplies for the ward
options.D: To register a new pharmacy business

explanation: The yellow form is the standard tool used by health workers to report unexpected or severe drug reactions to regulatory authorities. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is pharmacovigilance primarily concerned with?

options.A: Calculating hospital drug inventory levels
options.B: Manufacturing cheaper pharmaceutical products
options.C: Detecting and preventing adverse drug effects
options.D: Setting market prices for new medicines

explanation: Pharmacovigilance focuses on monitoring, assessing, and preventing harmful reactions linked to medication use in patients. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h1)

question: How does an adverse drug reaction differ from a predictable drug side effect?

options.A: It only happens when a patient overdoses intentionally
options.B: It is typically harmful and occurs at normal doses
options.C: It is always mild and requires no medical treatment
options.D: It has no relation to the pharmacological action

explanation: An adverse drug reaction is a noxious, unintended bodily response occurring at standard therapeutic doses. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which agency coordinates medication safety and post-market surveillance in Nigeria?

options.A: NMA
options.B: FMOH
options.C: NMNC
options.D: NAFDAC

explanation: NAFDAC is the national body responsible for regulating and monitoring the safety of food and drugs in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why are clinical trials insufficient for discovering every possible drug reaction?

options.A: They involve small sample sizes before public release
options.B: Pharmaceutical companies refuse to document adverse events
options.C: Participants never take medications as prescribed
options.D: Researchers deliberately hide dangerous drug side effects

explanation: Clinical trials test drugs on limited groups of people, meaning rare reactions only show up after widespread public use. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the common color designation of the NAFDAC ADR reporting form?

options.A: White
options.B: Yellow
options.C: Green
options.D: Blue

explanation: The NAFDAC adverse drug reaction reporting tool is traditionally recognized and referred to as the Yellow Form. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is the main advantage of using a standardized reporting form nationwide?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for patient interviews
options.B: It allows easy comparison and analysis of collected data
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of purchasing medications
options.D: It forces doctors to prescribe only locally made drugs

explanation: A uniform format ensures that reports from different health facilities contain the same vital information for safe review. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which specific drug detail is essential on an ADR form to trace counterfeit or faulty batches?

options.A: Pharmacy location
options.B: Import tax rate
options.C: Batch number
options.D: Manufacturer CEO

explanation: Recording the batch number helps regulatory authorities trace specific production runs if a widespread safety issue arises. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why must traditional or herbal remedies be listed under concomitant medications?

options.A: To check for potential herb-drug interactions
options.B: To satisfy traditional medicine practitioners
options.C: To find out where the patient bought herbs
options.D: To calculate the total cost of patient care

explanation: Herbal products can interact with orthodox medicines and trigger unexpected adverse reactions in the body. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient develops a severe skin rash two days after starting a new antibiotic. What is your first documentation step on the ADR form?

options.A: Record the reaction details and the suspected antibiotic
options.B: Write a formal letter to the national newspaper
options.C: Contact the pharmaceutical manufacturing company abroad
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately from the hospital ward

explanation: Documenting the exact reaction and the offending drug forms the core foundation of any valid pharmacovigilance report. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why is it necessary for the reporting nurse to include their professional contact details?

options.A: To allow regulatory officers to request clarification if needed
options.B: To update the patient's personal employment records
options.C: To ensure the nurse receives financial compensation for reporting
options.D: To prove that the hospital pharmacy has enough drug stock

explanation: Pharmacovigilance teams often need to follow up with the original reporter to gather missing clinical details. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h5)

question: What defines an adverse drug reaction as 'serious' in clinical reporting?

options.A: It results in death or prolongs hospitalization
options.B: It happens to patients over the age of sixty
options.C: It requires changing the drug brand name
options.D: It causes mild nausea for less than an hour

explanation: Serious adverse drug reactions involve life-threatening conditions, death, significant disability, or extended hospital stays. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of conducting a causality assessment on an ADR report?

options.A: To calculate the market price of the suspected drug
options.B: To determine if the drug actually caused the reaction
options.C: To check if the hospital pharmacy is running out of stock
options.D: To decide which nurse should care for the patient

explanation: Causality assessment evaluates the strength of the relationship between the medicine intake and the adverse event observed. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h6)

question: Where can completed paper ADR forms be submitted within Nigeria?

options.A: Commercial banks handling health insurance
options.B: Local police stations for criminal investigation
options.C: NAFDAC zonal offices or designated committees
options.D: Federal Ministry of Education headquarters

explanation: Completed reports are channeled through institutional drug committees or directly to NAFDAC zonal offices for processing. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h7)

question: What should a nurse do if new laboratory test results arrive after submitting an initial ADR report?

options.A: Throw away the old report and forget about the incident
options.B: Call the pharmaceutical manufacturer to demand a refund
options.C: Submit a follow-up report with the new clinical details
options.D: Wait until the patient is discharged to rewrite everything

explanation: Providing supplementary laboratory or outcome data ensures the safety database remains accurate and complete. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T6#GNS215_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why does under-reporting of adverse drug reactions remain a major challenge in clinical settings?

question: A patient complains of dizziness after taking a newly prescribed antihypertensive drug. What is the best nursing action?

question: What is the primary purpose of a Drug Revolving Fund in a health facility?

question: Who is primarily responsible for overseeing the day-to-day management and policies of a DRF?

question: Why are routine physical stock counts essential for sustaining a hospital drug revolving fund?

question: What is the primary goal of the Drug Revolving Fund pricing model in public health facilities?

question: Why does DRF pricing differ fundamentally from commercial retail pharmacy pricing?

question: Why is operational wastage factored into the basic cost components of DRF drugs?

question: What determines the percentage mark-up applied to DRF drugs in public facilities?

question: What happens to a Drug Revolving Fund when medications are consistently underpriced?

question: What is the primary goal of the Drug Revolving Fund model in hospitals?

question: Why do strict cash-and-carry drug schemes create problems for vulnerable patients?

question: A patient getting penicillin starts wheezing, has swollen lips, and feels dizzy. What is likely happening?

options.B: A severe allergic reaction affecting the whole body
options.C: A delayed skin reaction to the drug
options.D: Irritation right at the needle insertion spot

explanation: Simultaneous respiratory, skin, and cardiovascular symptoms point directly to systemic anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h4)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do if an acute drug reaction starts?

options.A: Stop the drug infusion immediately
options.B: Leave the bedside to call a doctor
options.C: Give an oral anti-allergy tablet
options.D: Write down what is happening in the patient's chart

explanation: Halting further administration of the causative agent stops ongoing systemic exposure. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why should the nurse keep the intravenous line open with normal saline after stopping the trigger drug?

options.A: To measure urine output through a catheter
options.B: To have a ready line for emergency fluids and medications
options.C: To wash out the mouth before giving oxygen
options.D: To dilute any remaining medicine in the stomach

explanation: An open IV line allows rapid administration of emergency medications and intravenous fluids for blood pressure support. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: How often should you check vital signs during an active, severe drug reaction?

options.A: Once every four hours as per routine
options.B: Once a day during morning handover
options.C: Only after the emergency drugs have finished working
options.D: Every few minutes until the patient is stable

explanation: Frequent interval tracking is essential to catch sudden hemodynamic shifts during acute reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: What does a fast heart rate and falling oxygen level mean during a drug reaction?

options.A: The heart and lungs are struggling
options.B: The patient is having a normal recovery
options.C: The patient is well hydrated and stable
options.D: The allergy medicine is working well

explanation: Tachycardia and desaturation reflect compensatory stress and failing respiratory function. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which drug is given first to treat sudden, severe anaphylaxis?

options.A: Paracetamol
options.B: Hydrocortisone
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Promethazine

explanation: Epinephrine is the essential first-line drug that reverses airway constriction and vascular collapse. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why is emergency epinephrine given into the thigh muscle instead of under the skin?

options.A: The thigh muscle has fewer nerve endings
options.B: Injections under the skin destroy muscle tissue
options.C: It is less painful for adults
options.D: It enters the bloodstream much faster from muscle

explanation: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis ensures rapid systemic absorption during emergencies. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which detail is NOT needed when writing an incident report for an acute drug reaction?

options.A: The exact time the symptoms started
options.B: The patient's home address and phone number
options.C: The exact name of the drug that caused the reaction
options.D: The emergency treatments given

explanation: Clinical documentation focuses on the incident specifics rather than demographic contact details. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)

question: Why do healthcare systems track and report adverse drug reactions?

options.A: To calculate hospital revenue and pharmacy stock
options.B: To punish nurses who make mistakes
options.C: To decide standard ward accommodation fees
options.D: To monitor drug safety trends across different hospitals

explanation: Pharmacovigilance reporting helps national bodies track adverse drug patterns and protect public health. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary factor determining the speed of systemic toxicity from a chemical exposure?

options.A: The route of exposure and concentration
options.B: The time of day the exposure occurred
options.C: The ambient room temperature during contact
options.D: The patient age and blood pressure

explanation: How the chemical enters the body and how much of it is present dictate how fast and severely it impacts internal organs. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h1)

question: An unconscious patient is brought in after inhaling an industrial solvent. Why is this route particularly dangerous?

options.A: It provides a massive surface area for rapid absorption
options.B: It bypasses the liver for immediate detoxification
options.C: It prevents any dermal or ocular irritation
options.D: It only affects the upper nasal passages

question: Which vital sign change is a common early indicator of severe chemical toxicity?

options.A: A gradual increase in body height over hours
options.B: A complete absence of any physical movement
options.C: Normal resting pulse and stable respiration
options.D: Sudden changes in heart rate or breathing rate

explanation: Vital sign instability, such as rapid breathing or abnormal pulse rates, signals that internal homeostatic systems are failing. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h2)

question: A patient exposed to an unknown chemical shows profound tachypnea. What does this sign most directly suggest?

options.A: The chemical has directly caused kidney failure
options.B: The chemical has caused pulmonary irritation or hypoxia
options.C: The patient has a chronic long-term bone infection
options.D: The patient is experiencing normal anxiety from the hospital

explanation: Rapid breathing frequently reflects the body trying to compensate for lack of oxygen or direct damage to the lung tissue. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h2)

question: What is the absolute first priority when assessing a patient with a severe chemical exposure?

options.A: Drawing baseline blood samples
options.B: Airway patency and protection
options.C: Writing an incident report
options.D: Checking deep tendon reflexes

question: Why is oral inspection critical during the initial airway assessment for a chemical burn victim?

options.A: To determine the exact brand of chemical ingested

options.C: To check for soot, burns, or swelling that threatens breathing
options.D: To measure the exact pH of the stomach contents

question: What does the term toxidrome refer to in emergency toxicology?

options.A: An antidote given to reverse heavy metal poisoning
options.B: A specialized machine used to filter toxins from blood
options.C: A legal document required after a chemical spill
options.D: A group of symptoms pointing to a specific class of poison

explanation: Recognizing grouped symptom patterns allows clinicians to identify broad chemical categories quickly before lab results return. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h4)

question: A farm worker exposed to pesticide presents with excessive drooling, tearing, and involuntary urination. Which toxidrome is present?

options.A: Anticholinergic toxidrome
options.B: Sedative-hypnotic toxidrome
options.C: Cholinergic toxidrome
options.D: Sympathomimetic toxidrome

question: Which type of chemical burn typically causes liquefaction necrosis and deep tissue penetration?

options.A: Pure water solutions
options.B: Acidic substances
options.C: Alkaline substances
options.D: Saline irrigations

explanation: Alkalis break down cell membranes and dissolve proteins, allowing them to seep deeper into tissues than most acids. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h5)

question: Why is immediate water irrigation prioritized over detailed eye exams for chemical splashes?

options.A: Water neutralizes the chemical pH automatically without testing
options.B: Prolonged contact increases the risk of permanent corneal damage
options.C: Eye exams are illegal without a specialized ophthalmologist present
options.D: Detailed exams require instruments that do not exist in clinics

question: Which diagnostic test is essential for evaluating acid-base balance in a severely poisoned patient?

options.A: Complete blood cell count
options.B: Routine urinalysis dipstick
options.C: Arterial blood gases
options.D: Standard chest radiograph

question: Why is continuous cardiac monitoring ordered for patients exposed to unknown chemicals?

options.A: It is the only way to measure blood pressure accurately
options.B: Cardiac telemetry speeds up the excretion of toxins through sweat
options.C: It replaces the need for a physical neurological exam
options.D: Many toxins can alter electrical conduction and cause fatal dysrhythmias
